transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
The Supreme Court has denied a last minute request
from the Trump administration to wade into its unprecedented
feud with California over the state's voter rolls.
NPR's Jude Joffe Block reports that denial comes just hours
after the Justice Department filed its appeal.
- The Justice Department wanted the High Court
to force California election officials
to set aside ballots that pertain to 20,000 people
that federal officials say are likely non-citizens.
But California election officials and data experts
have argued the DOJ's list is full of errors.
Plus, they've said segregating ballots isn't feasible
with voting already underway.
The Supreme Court's refusal to take on the case
comes after both a federal judge
and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected
the DOJ's demand last week,
citing that the Constitution gives state's authority
to run elections.
Plus, federal courts tend to avoid changing voting rules
right before an election.
Jude Joffe Block, NPR News.
- In the run up to midterm election day,
both parties have been spending millions of dollars
in advertising to reach voters.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reports on the races in focus.
- Millions of people have already cast their midterm ballots,
but millions of dollars are still being spent
to get people to vote on election day.
The money moves are both deep and wide.
Several races are seeing tens of millions
in last minute cash,
and the investment is going to long-time toss-up races
in Ohio, Iowa, Michigan, and Texas,
plus deeply conservative areas in places like Arkansas,
Tennessee, and Mississippi.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News, Des Moines, Iowa.
- Overseas, both Russia and Ukraine
say their country's public emergency alert systems
were hacked.
NPR's Charles Mains reports a result
was citizens receiving false warnings
of impending air raids and even nuclear attacks.
- Ukraine's public air raid app
began sending false alerts late Sunday,
with varying messages warning of a chemical weapons attack
and high radiation levels,
even an incoming strike by a nuclear-capable missile.
Ukraine's air force quickly assured the public
that claims were false and accused Russia
of being behind the stunt.
Meanwhile, on Monday, Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry
said one of its alert systems had been compromised.
Russians received messages claiming the country
was under nuclear attack and advising residents
to stock up on food and take cover underground.
Yet the hackers used language
not typical of official communiques.
A factor officials in both countries
said limited public panic.
Charles Mains, NPR News.
- U.S. Special Envoy Steve Whitcomb says the U.S.
will mediate talks between Ukraine and Russia next week,
and a social media post,
Whitcomb said the talks will take place in Abu Dhabi.
Russia agreed last month to resume three-way negotiations,
setting up the first talks on ending wars since February.
This is NPR News.
In Southwest Colorado, a second round of severe flooding
has forced evacuations and damaged roads and businesses,
Colorado Public Radio's Haley May reports.
- In the mountain town of Durango,
near the Four Corners region,
floodwaters have turned residential streets into rivers.
Bryant's Liget lives on the edge of an evacuation zone
where water surged through neighborhoods
near the Animas River.
- Probably like a maybe 10, 15 block radius
that did have knee-high water running down the streets,
just replaced the streets with water.
- As residents prepare for cleanup,
officials are asking the recreation-heavy town
to stay out of the water,
as fears surrounding large debris and toxins
or sharp objects in the water mount.
The rain has stopped,
but officials say the damage is far from over.
For NPR News, I'm Haley May in Denver.
- Authorities and flagstaffs say two people
are believed to have died
as a result of major flooding Sunday,
and evacuations are in effect
for several Arizona communities.
Governor Katie Hobbs has declared a state of emergency,
and the governors of New Mexico and Colorado
are asking President Trump to declare a major disaster
to receive funding assistance.
The fraud trial of Cleveland Guardian's pitchers,
Emmanuel Closay and Luis Ortiz, is underway in New York.
The two are charged with colluding with gamblers
who made hundreds of thousands of dollars
betting on individual pitches.
Both have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges
and are on non-disciplinary leave from their club
without pay.
Jury selection started Monday in Brooklyn Federal Court.
I'm Jael Snyder, NPR News.

topics.text: Supreme Court denies Trump administration's request to intervene in California voter rolls dispute
Both parties spend tens of millions on last-minute midterm ads in Ohio, Iowa, Michigan, Texas
Ukraine and Russia say their public emergency alert systems were hacked, sending false attack warnings
Severe flooding in Durango, Colorado forces evacuations and damages roads and businesses
Two believed dead and evacuations ordered in Arizona after major Sunday flooding; governors seek federal aid
Fraud trial begins in Brooklyn for Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz
